title: Inside a Web Server
description: Walk through exactly what happens when a browser hits a web server — from socket accept to response, covering threading models and middleware.

segments.text: Ever wonder what actually happens when you type a URL and hit Enter? Today we're going to follow that request from the moment it arrives at the server to the moment the response goes back. Let's open the hood.

A web server starts by creating a socket and binding it to a port — usually port 80 or 443. Then it listens. Think of it as opening a shop door and putting up an 'Open' sign. The server sits there, waiting for customers.

When a client connects, the server calls accept, which creates a brand-new socket just for that conversation. The original socket keeps listening for more customers. It's like a receptionist handing you off to a dedicated clerk.
The server reads raw bytes from that socket and parses them into an HTTP request — method, path, headers, body. 'GET /api/users HTTP/1.1' becomes structured data the application can work with.

Next comes routing — matching the request path to the right handler function. Think of it as a switchboard operator connecting your call. GET /users goes to the user handler, POST /orders goes to the order handler.
Now here's the big question. While the server is handling your request, what happens if another client connects? The server can't just ignore new customers while serving one.
segments.thought_prompt: How would you handle thousands of simultaneous connections with just one CPU?

segments.text: The classic model: thread-per-request. Each incoming connection gets its own thread. Simple and intuitive — like hiring a new waiter for every table. But threads are expensive. At ten thousand connections, you've got ten thousand threads eating memory and fighting for CPU.

The alternative: an event loop. One thread handles many connections by never blocking. Instead of waiting for a database response, it says 'call me back when it's ready' and goes to serve another request. Node.js made this model famous.

Before your request reaches the handler, it typically passes through middleware — a pipeline of functions. Authentication checks, logging, rate limiting, body parsing. Each middleware can modify the request, reject it, or pass it along. Think of it as airport security checkpoints.

Middleware order matters a lot. If you put your authentication check after your logging middleware, you'll log sensitive requests from unauthenticated users. Small ordering decisions can have security implications.
segments.thought_prompt: Where would you place rate-limiting middleware in the pipeline — early or late? Why?

segments.text: Finally, the handler does its work — queries a database, applies business logic — and constructs a response. Status code, headers, body. The server serializes it back to bytes and writes it to the socket. The circle is complete.

Socket accept, parse, route, middleware, handle, respond — that's the lifecycle of every web request. The choice between thread-per-request and event loop fundamentally shapes your server's performance characteristics. Keep this mental model; it'll serve you well as we scale up.
